newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: FOCUS-Philippine peso near lows but stocks rise.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Philippine peso near lows but stocks rise.

text.p: Financial markets in the Philippines were a study in contrasts on Friday as the peso hovered near a 27-month low and the stock market rose for the fifth straight day.
Analysts said the currency's fall was temporary, brought about by speculation after a reduction in domestic interest rates was triggered by a reserve requirement cut last week.
The stock market rise mirrored the positive impact of lower interest rates and expectations of lower inflation, they added.
Jose Salceda, a director at SBC Warburg, said although the peso was falling, it still reflected positive fundamentals since it was trading within a narrow band.
He said a positive outlook on inflation indicated the currency would not weaken further.
"I wouldn't be myopic about the peso," he said.
Analysts expect 1997 inflation to be about 6.5 percent this year from 8.4 percent in 1996.
Although pulled down by a narrower interest rate premium over the U.S. dollar, the peso's move was also driven by the projected wider trade deficit this year, analysts said.
"It should depreciate. That's going to help exports," said Peter Mutuc, managing director of HG Asia Securities.

Philippine Central Bank governor Gabriel Singson has said the country's widening trade deficit should not be cause for alarm since it did not suggest loss of export competitiveness or excessive consumption.

The Central Bank said the wider trade deficit was due to heavy capital equipment imports of expanding industries. Analysts say the trade gap could grow to $14.0 billion this year from an estimated $12.0 billion last year.

The peso traded on Thursday and most of Friday at a 27-month low at 26.345 to the dollar as a number of nervous offshore funds closed out their positions after the reserve requirement cut enhanced peso liquidity and sent interest rates plunging.

On Friday, the peso closed at 26.337 after the Central Bank maintained a steady selling rate of 26.345 and the demand for dollars abated, partly because of an inflow of foreign funds into the stock market, dealers said.
The stock market rose 2.9 percent, or 92.88 points, in the week to close at 3,262.14 on Friday.
"Our fighting target for the stock market is 3,650 points in the first quarter," said SBC Warburg's Salceda.

Based on its own basket, SBC Warburg estimated the market was trading at 17 times forecast 1997 corporate earnings, near the low of its usual trading band from 16 to 22 times, while its neighbouring markets in southeast Asia were trading at 14 times.
"I think the premium should be wider for the Philippine market. We're the only ones accelerating," Salceda said.
He cited the Philippines as the only economy in the region that posted a 29.8 percent growth in exports in November, while the rest were sluggish.

HG Asia's Mutuc said the Philippines was expected to register one of the highest corporate earnings growth in the region at 25 percent this year, compared with 23 percent in Indonesia and 17 percent each in Malaysia and Thailand.

A prominent Filipino banker said on Friday that domestic interest rates would have to rise in order to cushion the peso's fall given that U.S. interest rates are bound to go up in coming months due to the perceived strength of its economy.
"The moment that the differential has narrowed to a certain point, something has to give," Bankers Association of the Philippines president Rafael Buenaventura said.

"(The Central Bank) has to factor in the interest rate of the United States and the interest rates elsewhere because there are alternative outlets (for investors)," he said. "It's a tough balancing act."
